title: The Long Field
subtitle: A Novel of the Fens
description: Cambridgeshire, 1911. The wet spring threatens to undo Nell Askew, who has spent two years holding her late husband's forty acres of black peat against the water. Now the drainage board wants to cut a new dyke through the long field, the only land that pays. Philip Danvers, the surveyor, arrives with his notebook and careful courtesy. Nell's brother-in-law urges her to sell and move to Ely. Her daughter wants the world to stay unchanged. Only Amos Reed, the hired man who came back from the Boer War silent, stands with her. From Lady Day to harvest, the weather and the water table do the work of fate. The pump, the cut, the market, the chapel, the flooded road. No villain, only the dyke coming. A novel of what people decide to keep.

editorReview.text: The sensory immersion in the fen landscape is exceptional; you feel the cold go through Nell’s shawl “like a hand,” anchoring her struggle against the black peat in a visceral, unforgettable way. The lamb-birthing sequence stands out as a masterclass in immediate, mortal stakes. However, the prose occasionally falls into mechanical rhythms—repetitive sentence openings flatten the texture that the scene-setting works so hard to build. Furthermore, a late-stage exposition dump compresses decades of history too tightly, rushing what should be a gradual reveal. It is a powerful, atmospheric read,
editorReview.title: Fiction Editor
